title: Salsifis à la crème
subtitle: Salsify in cream sauce
excerpt: Salsify roots boiled, then finished in a simple cream and lemon sauce. An old-fashioned French winter vegetable dish with a delicate, slightly oyster-like flavour that is worth seeking out.
sourceNotes: Salsifis à la crème is a classic French vegetable preparation documented in Escoffier's Le Guide Culinaire (1903), where salsify (salsifis) appears in multiple preparations including à la crème and à la poulette. Larousse Gastronomique (1938) also includes the dish. Both are widely available as public-domain or historical culinary references.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The salsify can be boiled a few hours ahead. Finish in the cream sauce just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A long, slender root vegetable with a pale skin and white flesh. Its flavour is mild and slightly reminiscent of oysters, which is why it is sometimes called the 'oyster plant'. Used in French cooking boiled, creamed, or gratinéed.

content.text: Salsify is an old French winter vegetable that fell out of fashion and deserves to come back. Once peeled and boiled, its flesh is soft, white, and mild with an undertone that French cooks compare to oysters. À la crème is the simplest and most satisfying way to serve it: the cooked roots are tossed in cream that reduces lightly around them, seasoned with lemon juice, and served as a side dish alongside roast meat or pan-fried fish.

items.prepNote: peeled and cut into 5 cm lengths, dropped immediately into acidulated water

content.text: Drain the salsify from the acidulated water. Cook in well-salted boiling water for 20 to 25 minutes until completely tender when pierced with a knife. Drain thoroughly.

Melt the butter in a wide saucepan over medium heat. Add the drained salsify and toss gently for 2 minutes. Pour in the double cream and let it bubble and reduce for 3 to 4 minutes until it coats the salsify in a light sauce.
Add a squeeze of lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper. Scatter with chopped parsley and serve immediately.

items.cause: Not put into acidulated water quickly enough
items.fix: Work fast and have the acidulated water ready before you pick up the peeler. The discolouration is purely cosmetic; the flavour is unaffected.

items.cause: Older roots can take longer to cook
items.fix: Keep cooking until the salsify is completely soft. Check every 5 minutes. Hard salsify is not pleasant to eat.

content.text: Salsify was a staple of the French winter table from the seventeenth century through to the early twentieth, appearing in market gardens throughout the Paris basin and the Loire Valley. It fell from fashion when more convenient vegetables such as frozen peas and tinned haricots became widely available, but it has never disappeared from the markets in northern France, where it is still sold from November through to February. It is served alongside game birds, braised beef, and roast pork in the traditional French kitchen. The cream preparation is the most classic.
